title: Screens, Social Media and Online Safety
reflection: When my child reaches for a screen, what might they be looking for, and how could they find more of it at home?

questions.q: According to Lesson 17, why does a feed pull so strongly on a young mind?
o: Children lack the character to resist, and need firmer rules to make up for it.
Waves arrive unsettled, the reaching becomes a habit, and the pull is built in.
The content is harmful in itself, and each hour of it leaves lasting damage.
The feed fills a child’s empty time, and any other activity would work as well.
questions.e: The mind takes the shape of whatever attention rests on, and a feed sends such waves without end. Attention scatters, a groove forms in the reaching for the next thing, and the pull is built in by those who design feeds. None of this is a failing of character; the current pulls on wise adults as much as on children.
questions.c: The mind takes the shape of the feed; the pull is built in

questions.q: A mother sees a line of light under her twelve-year-old daughter’s door at midnight, and the daughter says, “Everyone’s on it, Mum.” Which approach fits Lesson 17?
o: Take the phone away at once, since sleep matters more than what is on it.
Explain how feeds are built to hold attention, and leave the choice to her.
Say nothing until she is older, since children resent being managed.
Read the light as a clue to what she seeks, and meet that need at home.
questions.e: Every child has needs of the heart: to be noticed, listened to, enjoyed and to belong. When these are not met at home, a child looks for them through the screen. The feed is also a mirror: what a child seeks there shows the hunger underneath, and a parent who reads it can meet it. Phones sleeping outside the bedroom helps too.
questions.c: The screen shows the hunger; meet the need at home

questions.q: In the lesson’s picture of the monkey-mind, what does watching the mind do?
o: As the watching goes on, the restlessness grows less and the mind quietens.
It drives the restless thoughts away, so that the mind is left empty and still.
It punishes the monkey for leaping, so that it learns not to jump again.
It tires the mind, which then stops reaching for lack of energy.
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda’s way is not to fight the monkey but to watch it. Sit quietly, let the mind jump, and simply watch; the restlessness grows less and less. The monkey is not driven away or punished; under a steady, patient gaze it becomes calm. Each time a child draws in by choice, they discover they are not their impulses.
questions.c: Watch the monkey; do not fight it

questions.q: A seven-year-old cries and shouts when the tablet is switched off at bedtime. Which view fits Lesson 17?
o: He is being defiant, and the limit must be held more firmly than before.
The tablet is the enemy, and it should be removed from the house.
His mind had taken the shape of the game; hold the limit calmly and warmly.
The limit is too strict, and a later bedtime would end the tears.
questions.e: Being asked to stop feels like a loss, because the mind had taken the very shape of the game. The protest is that wave being broken, not defiance. The device is neutral; the power is in the mind. The parent holds the limit with calm and warmth, and a few minutes of watching the monkey together can help him learn to draw in.
questions.c: The protest is a wave being broken, not defiance

questions.q: “Screens are the enemy of childhood, so the safest course is to keep children away from them entirely.”
questions.e: The device is neutral; the power is in the mind. That a small screen can hold a mind so completely shows how great the power of attention is. The screen also brings real gifts: family far away kept close, a lonely child finding others who understand, any subject open to a curious mind. The task is to gather attention, not to fear the device.
questions.c: The device is neutral; gather the attention

questions.q: A parent wants fewer battles over screens at home. Which approach fits Lesson 17?
o: Make a long list of rules, so that every case is covered in advance.
Agree a few clear rules together, apply them to adults too, and model them.
Keep the rules for the children only, since adults have different needs.
Apply the rules strictly and leave the reasons to be understood in time.
questions.e: Example is the water and rules are the banks. The rules that hold best are few, clear and agreed together: where devices sleep, which times are screen-free, what comes first after school. Let the children propose some, and let the rules apply to the adults too. A rule reaches the ears; an example reaches the whole child.
questions.c: Example is the river, and a few agreed rules the banks

questions.q: Why does Lesson 17 say that controls and settings on a device should give way over the years?
o: Older children can always find a way around them, and so they stop working.
They are useful only for the youngest, since older children know the risks well.
They are a sign of distrust, and distrust always harms the bond with a child.
They are scaffolding; the aim is a child who chooses well unwatched.
questions.e: They are tools, and tools have their season. For young children, a parent holds the limits and settings help. As children grow, the tools give way, step by step, to trust and the young person’s own judgement, like scaffolding lowered as a building stands on its own. The aim of every rule is to become unnecessary.
questions.c: Tools give way to trust and the child’s own judgement

questions.q: A thirteen-year-old tells her mother that a stranger online has been asking her for pictures. Which response fits Lesson 17?
o: Thank her, say she is not in trouble, listen, then keep the messages, block and report.
Ask first why she replied to the stranger, so that she understands her part in it.
Take away her phone at once, so that the contact stops for good.
Reply to the stranger firmly, and tell him to stay away from her daughter.
questions.e: The first moments decide whether she will ever tell again: take a breath, keep the face soft, thank her, listen fully and say she is not in trouble. The one who pressured her is responsible, not the child. Then act calmly: do not reply or pay, keep the messages without forwarding any picture of the child, block and report, and tell the police or the online safety service.
questions.c: Thank her, stay calm, then act: keep, block, report

questions.q: “Good filters and strict rules can prevent nearly everything that goes wrong online, so the main job is to set them up.”
questions.e: No rule and no filter can prevent all of it; sooner or later something will go wrong online for almost every child. What protects a child most is that, when it does, they come home and tell. The door is kept open by calm in small troubles, light conversations about online life, and the promise that telling will never cost the phone.
questions.c: What protects most is a child who comes home and tells

questions.q: A fourteen-year-old has seemed low and frightened for several weeks since a cruel online episode, though her parents have been warm and calm. Which step fits Lesson 17?
o: Give it more time, since a mind settles by itself once the cause has passed.
Take the phone away until she is feeling well again.
Keep the door open, and also seek a doctor or counsellor to help.
Teach her the watching practice daily, and expect it to be enough.
questions.e: If a child seems low, frightened or not themselves for weeks after something online, a doctor or counsellor can help, alongside everything the parent does at home. Every safety step matters and none is the whole answer; the deepest protection is a child whose heart is anchored at home, with somewhere safe to return.
questions.c: Care and home together; the heart anchored at home
